Hasn't it been more of a cycle that runs from centralization to decentralization? When we go from large empires, to multiple nation states, to super powers, is it so crazy to think the next step is another swing towards decentralization?

The advent of the state itself presupposed centralization. And the state, properly speaking, did not exist before the modern era.

Large empires have not necessitated centralization. For example, the Achaemenid Empire was little more than a conglomeration of tribes that kept their own ways and traditions but pledged allegiance to the sovereign. A nation-state like Prussia was far more centralized. Centralization, one should bear in mind, becomes more possible with greater advances in technology - advanced technology was not exactly something one associates with ancient empires.

But to speak directly to the point: centralized nations tend to come into being to defend themselves from rivals. This was how Germany became a unified nation: fear of France. Even the US united to defend itself from Britain. And this imperative for unity still exists. If we break up the country into a jillion company towns the end result will be some powerful entity on our soil.

I guess if we accept that long term trends are a certain way because of natural evolution, we could say that a centralized state global state is inevitable. There is are limits, that vary from person to person, on what they deem acceptable in terms of centralization or regulation. At what point, if at any, does the population demand decentralization? Does one just accept that there is no way to reverse the trend? Is there any chance given new technologies? Some technology like 3D printers could revolutionize multiple industries, and lead to small manufactures of basic parts, pieces or tools. At the same time technology allows an easier form of surveillance. Is anarcho-capitalism impossible because it goes against the trend, or is it something more?

A one world government strikes me as unlikely barring a threat from space aliens or something. Why would it occur otherwise?

We may see some form of decentralization. We have with Brexit. But these things come about due to powerful historical forces not ideological rigidity. I guess the best one can hope for is to set up a model and hope history eventually moves in one's direction.

I'm a libertarian and I (mostly) agree with you. I think it's important for libertarians to support incremental steps in the right direction. But it's also essential to be committed to the revolutionary ideal of abolishing the political state as a system, and to give voice to that ideal.

Some things I have to argue with:

I'm for open borders, for tommorow. I want strong borders today.

I think that using the term "open borders" to describe the libertarian goal is misleading. (I'm assuming that our disagreement here is only semantic, but maybe it's not.)

I oppose the minimum wage, but let's tackle corporate welfare first.

Let's tackle whichever we have the chance to tackle first. There's no connection between these two particular issues that would make it preferable to deal with them in that order. Abolishing the minimum wage will benefit the poorest and most vulnerable; if we could do it then why should we delay?

The FDA should be abolished, but there should be multiple competing private agencies operating before the FDA is dissolved.

Why? And how would these private agencies get started if they had to "compete" with an agency backed by the power and tax revenues of the federal government?

Open borders definitely means the free flow of goods and services, and I can support that. I can support regulated immigration ad well. A basically non-existent border seems like a bad idea until neighboring countries can achieve a similar level on economic status.

As far as minimum wage versus corporate welfare: The comparison is meant to demonstrate a sense of pragmatism. It seems easier to have the general population support an end to corporate welfare. I don't see the eradication of the minimum wage gaining support, and theoretically undoing regulations and barriers to entry would make a minimum wage obsolete.

It isn't impossible to compete against a government agency. The post office competes with FedEx and UPS. The biggest advantage the post office has is a monopoly on first class mail. I know the comparison isn't perfect. There isn't an oligarchy of carrier services with a revolving door in and out of the post master general's office. Essentially allowing the FDA to act as it currently does, and allowing competitors to review drugs and food, wpuld create the new system in the shell of the old. I could easily see confidence drop in the food and drug market without some kind of service offering a review process/certification.

Anarchy is the natural state of things and so the best way for it to come into being is through a more natural route. Anarchy's main problem is that the natural route is often interfered with by aggression, i.e., there is often either a lack of peace within or outside the borders. So for Anarchy to become sustainable it needs time to grow, protected from the harm of interference until it can become firmly rooted and produce fruitful results. I believe at that point it will have the means to deal with such issues as the public defense, people owning nukes, etc, but that's a rabbit trail I don't want to go down at the moment.

So what I suggest would be to set up an interim government. This government would have a constitution which laid out an obnoxiously clear goal: the very eradication of its own existence over time. Two primary goals of this constitution would be to take whatever the past system of government was and privatize everything in stages and to give back all the rights of the people that had been taken away. This would be done so as to not shock the economy or the populous with drastic changes and to not leave room for destabilizing forces to thrive.
